items.text: On one rented GPU node, does the cost of direct simulation grow as Reynolds number to the sixth power, and does finer resolution remove the error a turbulence model leaves?
Compute buys fidelity for small-scale statistics that closures discard, while cheap closures stay cheaper for large-scale quantities at modest Reynolds number.

Fully resolved simulation matches the published 1024^3 statistics within tolerance. Unmodeled simulation error in velocity-gradient statistics falls as grid size N grows, while large-eddy simulation keeps an error floor.
Smagorinsky LES matches gradient statistics at equal cost, or resolved DNS misses the published statistics, so extra resolution does not remove closure error.

Build a GPU spectral turbulence solver, reproduce the published 1024^3 Johns Hopkins statistics, then measure cost per turnover versus Reynolds number and compare no-model DNS against Smagorinsky LES at fixed viscosity [jhtdb_readme].

JHTDB published 1024^3, 4096^3 and 8192^3 forced isotropic DNS statistics; largest reproduction here is 2048^3 versus their 8192^3 [jhtdb_readme]. No cost-versus-closure measurement on rented GPUs is cited.
Dollar cost per turnover on rented GPUs and whether Smagorinsky LES keeps an error floor in gradient statistics against the same-viscosity DNS.
Reproduce the published 1024^3 forced isotropic run: Taylor-scale Reynolds number 418, averaged over at least 10 turnover times [jhtdb_readme]

Reaches Taylor-scale Reynolds number about 420, perhaps 660 briefly; cannot move the research frontier. Cost figures are model estimates until the benchmark phase measures them. The reference describes the forcing in one sentence, so box size and large-eddy turnover time may differ by a few percent.

items.note: Rλ = 418 and the 1024^3 grid are confirmed on the page. But 'averaged over at least 10 turnover times' is contradicted: the published statistics are time-averaged over t = 0 to 10.056 simulation time units with T_L = 1.99, i.e. about 5 large-eddy turnover times, and the item's own recorded quote says 'The duration of the stored data is about five large-eddy turnover times.' The '10' appears to be the 10.056 time units mistaken for turnover times. If the plan instead means its own reproduction will average over >= 10 turnover times, that is a plan choice, but as written with the citation it misdescribes the published run.

items.text: At 1.5 degrees on a $1,000 budget, does GraphCast-style forecast skill improve more from 4 times the training compute or from 4 times the years of reanalysis data?
Quadrupling compute at 40 years improves day-5 Z500 RMSE more than quadrupling data from 10 to 40 years, because the 40-year record is near saturation [arXiv 2212.12794].
The day-5 Z500 RMSE gain from 4x compute at 40 years exceeds the gain from 4x data at full compute by more than twice the seed noise.
D exceeds C by more than twice the seed noise (data-bound), or neither exceeds the other by that margin (inconclusive).

Train ten GraphCast-style models at 1.5 degrees on one 8x H100 machine, varying years of ERA5 data (5 to 40) and compute (1/4 to 1x). Compare day-5 Z500 error gains from compute and data against seed noise and WB2 baselines.

GraphCast's authors found adding 1959-1978 data had little benefit, and ArchesWeather found older ERA5 harder to fit; neither varied years of data against compute under one setup [arXiv 2212.12794, 2405.14527].

items.page_quote: In preliminary work, we also explored training on earlier data from 1959–1978, but found it had little benefit on performance, so in the final phases of our work we excluded 1959–1978 for simplicity.
items.note: GraphCast claim verified verbatim (Supplements 4.1). ArchesWeather (arXiv 2405.14527, named in the text though absent from the sources array; fetched at arxiv.org/html/2405.14527) says: 'we find that forecasting models have a larger error in the first half of the training period 1979-2018, which we attribute to ERA5 being less constrained in the past due to a lack of observation data' - a fair basis for 'older ERA5 harder to fit'. Neither paper varies years of data against compute: GraphCast varies only the end year ('training data that always began in 1979, but ended in 2017, 2018, 2019, and 2020'); ArchesWeather trains on 1979-2018 and fine-tunes on 2007-2018.

items.page_quote: we trained four variants of GraphCast, with training data that always began in 1979, but ended in 2017, 2018, 2019, and 2020, respectively
items.note: The stated gap (matched years-vs-compute comparison, same architecture/evaluation, 1.5 degrees) is consistent with both fetched papers: GraphCast varies only recency at 0.25 degrees; ArchesWeather (1.5 degrees) trains on a fixed 1979-2018 window. The remark that the producer's web search was exhausted is a process note, not checkable against any page.

The cited netCDF (HTTP 200, 1,433,484 bytes, NetCDF 64-bit offset) gives GraphCast global day-5 2m_temperature RMSE = 1.251719, matching 1.252. It also gives GraphCast global day-5 Z500 RMSE = 274.25 (not claimed). The file contains only GraphCast-vs-ERA5 metrics (rmse/mse/bias/acc/prediction_activity/vector_rmse/seeps over 34 regions, 40 lead times, levels 500/700/850); the HRES T2M = 1.334 and HRES Z500 = 304.35 values are not in it, so two of the three anchor numbers are unverifiable from the cited source. The claim that 'our evaluation code reproduces' these is about the producer's own run and cannot be checked against a page.

scores.reason: Turbulence DNS cost and closure error say little about robot manipulation; contact and cloth physics are not tested, so the root choice barely changes.
Grid 128 to 2048 is 16x, resolution is bought with compute, and viscosity and forcing are fixed. Noise-versus-effect margin is only partly stated.
Reproduces the published JHTDB 1024^3 Re_lambda 418 within 4%, plus exact Taylor-Green solutions as truth independent of the method.
JHTDB publishes DNS up to 8192^3, so the prior covers more range; the cost-versus-closure gap on rented GPUs is stated.
Method is none; multi-GPU slab decomposition only splits state within each step, leaving time stepping in order.
restructuring.method is none, so baseline does not apply.

critique.decides_by_reason: The decision_rule needs the reproduction (p3) and the no-model DNS versus LES error comparison across N, which is first complete at p5. p4 alone lacks LES.

scores.reason: Weather emulator at 1.5 degrees; says nothing direct about robotics contact data. Outcomes bear on the robotics choice only by analogy.
Compute spans 4x, not 10x; data is also varied, so compute is not the only change. Noise rule and held_fixed are fine.
Scored against ERA5 truth, and the anchor reproduces published WB2 scores within a stated 0.5% tolerance.
Closest prior varied data only, not against compute; gap is stated, though a search may have missed a reproduction.
Method is none; one job per GPU runs independent copies side by side, with no dependency removed.
restructuring.method is none, so baseline timing does not apply.

critique.decides_by_reason: C, D and N all come from the main grid's runs. Staging and pilot only check gates and throughput, and scoring is CPU analysis afterward.
